cylindrical bole and no buttress. The bark is smooth and thin. It exudes abundant 
cream coloured latex which dries to a small ball if rubbed between the fingers. 
The leaves are broadly oval, opposite, dark green and leathery. Flowers are 
yellow-white, fragrant, and in dense shoot groups. Fruits develop as a pair of 
woody, flat follicles of 30cm. Seeds have long white hairs at one end. 
Propagation:  It is propagated from seeds and wildlings.

Lovoa trichiliodes/L. brownii : Lovoa trichiliodes/L. brownii : An evergreen tree of 
40m in height. The trunk is straight or wavy with a small or spreading dark crown. 
Buttresses usually absent, but the trunk may spread out at the base.  The bark is 
thin and smooth, brown, and sometimes dark and fissured in older trees, strongly 
scented if cut. Leaves; even pinnate on stalks to 24cm, stalk flat or winged 
between leaflet pairs, 6-12 leaflets, the same size at the base, about 10cm long 
with about 20 closely spaced side veins each side.  Small white flowers are 
abundant in large heads of 30cm. The fruit is present as a brown hanging capsule.  
Propagation: It is propagated from seeds and wildings. 
Uses: Firewood, timber (furniture, doors, windows), charcoal and ornamental.  
 
Markhamia platycalyx (Bignomaceae family): Slender boled tree of 24m in height. 
Its stem is fluted towards the base; the crown is irregular, and the bark is 
grey/brown and flaking in irregular strips and patches. Leaves; compound pinnate 
with 7-11 leaflets, often in bunches, thin and wavy, each leaflets to 10 cm, wider at 
the tip. . Flowers; Bright yellow clusters, each trumpet shaped with orange red 
strips in the throat, buds furry, splitting in one side.. The fruit capsule grows up to 
1.2 m long and 1.9 cm broad, with oblong seeds about 2.5 cm long including the 
yellow to white wood wings. 
Propagation: It is propagated from seeds and wildlings.

1.11 Identification of risks that may substantially affect the project’s GHG 
emission reductions or removal enhancements: 
 
Non-permanence risk assessment was carried out using the VCS’  “AFOLU Non-
Permanence Risk Tool” version 3 of 8 March 2011.  According to this tool, the 
project activity was rated at a low risk after yielding a 8.5% of buffer requirement. 
The project has a system in place to identify risks and established targets to 
reduce any non-permanent risks. Procedures have been developed and 
responsibilities are well assigned with internal auditing, reviews and training in 
place.  The project also has a well qualified, experienced local management team 
in place to ensure that the project activities are implemented effectively.  The land 
planned for the project activity is wholly contained within a national park.  Based 
on the Sections 3,4 and 5 of the Uganda Wildlife Statute, the national park is fully 
owned by the government of Uganda under the UWA Act and mandated by 
Uganda Wildlife Authority on behalf of Uganda government and all Ugandans. 
Therefore, UWA has full control over the entire project lands. Additionally, the 
project will hold a 10%  VCS buffer in reserve for use in case of any loss of 
permanence.

1.12 Demonstration to confirm that the project was not implemented to 
create GHG emissions primarily for the purpose of its subsequent 
removal or destruction.  
 
 At the time the project started, in 1995, carbon credits were not a commodity and 
the concept was unheard of. Face became involved in 1994 and did not invest in 
forest destruction but in forest restoration. Instead, deforestation that took place 
in the UWA-Face project area was as a result of  encroachment by local  
communities in the period between 1970 and 1985 (Okonya, 1993). For almost  30 
years local communities were farming within the Forest Reserve, grazing cattle, 
growing maize and bananas. There was no productively managed forest in the 
area. In 1993 all inhabitants and encroachers within the boundaries of the National 
Park were were re-settled  in Kibaale District,  approximately 100 km from Kibale 
National Park (FSC, 2010; General Management Plan of Kibale National Park, 2003-
2013).  These statements are further substantiated by the Figures 1.7.1 and 1.7.2 
presented earlier in the PD. 
 
The purpose of the project is to reforest degraded lands and to promote natural 
regeneration. The project was not implemented to create GHG emissions hence 
no clearing of forest for creation of VCU’s took place.

of the identified baseline scenario:

The “Combined tool to identify the baseline scenario and demonstrate 
additionality in ARR CDM project activities” is used to both identify  the baseline 
scenario. As will be demonstrated in Section 2.5, the most likely baseline scenario

UWA would have limited success in keeping encroachers at bay. This would mean that 
fires continue to roam the formerly encroached land and the carbon stock would be the 
result of a mix between agricultural activities, fire and partial regeneration of pioneer 
vegetation (grass and shrubs). The carbon stock in this case would be for the mix of 
shrub, forest and banana plantations.

STEP 0: Preliminary screening based on the starting date of the ARR project 
activity 
 
The proposed ARR VCS project was started in 1995 and since then, it has applied 
an externally reviewed methodology and engaged independent carbon 
monitoring experts to assess and quantify the project’s baseline scenario and net 
emissions reductions or removals resulting in carbon crediting under the SGS 
standard. In 2003 Face contracted the certification Société Générale de 
Surveillance (SGS) to validate and verify Kibale, based on SGS’ GHG Validation and 
Verification program. In the absence of an international standard defined or 
accepted by the UNFCCC Secretariat, SGS had prepared a set of criteria based on 
Decision 17/C.P7 of the Marrakech accords. These criteria act as a standard and the 
Kibale project was validated against it twice: in 2003 and 2008 respectively. 
Reports of these assessments were published in 2004 and 2009. Since then, 
project activity has been geared towards future crediting under VCS.  The 
incentive of planned sale of GHG emission allowances is evidenced in the steps 
further below of the additionality test. Without the GHG allowance sales, the 
project would not be economically attractive, and would face significant barriers.  
 
STEP 1: Identification of alternative land use scenarios to the proposed ARR VCS 
project activity 
 
Sub-step 1a: Identification of credible alternative land use scenarios to the project 
activity 
Since the lands to be planted are restricted to forestry purposes by government, 
other land uses are practically impossible, therefore the identified alternative land 
uses include three that were historically possible and one that relates to 
afforestation as recommended by the tool.

1. Continued encroachment at a scale and rate  of before project activities 
started 1993 This alternative comprises of a mix of grassland, shrub land 
and banana plantations.  
2. Continued but less intensive encroachment, assuming that UWA would 
have limited success in keeping encroachers at bay. This would mean that 
fires continue to roam the formerly encroached land and the carbon stock 
would be the result of a mix between agricultural activities, fire and partial 
regeneration of pioneer vegetation (grass, shrubs and bananas).  
3. No human encroachment, assuming that the park would have some 
success in protecting the area, but no investment in forest rehabilitation, 
while widespread and frequent perturbation by fire continues.  The 
resulting fire regime would favour elephant grass which would in turn 
suppress natural regeneration of trees.

STEP 2: Barrier analysis 
 
Sub-step 2a: Identification of  barriers that would prevent  the implementation of 
at least one alternative land use scenarios:  
There are no barriers related to continuation of land use scenarios 1-3 because 
there is no investment, institutional or technological barriers related to 
continuation of encroachment. However, alternative land use 4 faces the 
following barriers, which prohibit it from getting implemented in the absence of 
income derived from the sale of carbon credits derived from the Project Activity. 
These barriers include: 
  
a) Investment barriers: 
This project faces investment barriers, which prohibit its implementation without 
income derived from the sale of carbon credits or external donors. The main 
source of income for the Kibale National Park is derived from tourism activities 
while that of neighboring communities comes from subsistence agriculture, with 
poor access to improved agricultural implements and limited market access. 
Hence, neither UWA nor the local communities have the ability to invest in ARR 
project activities since VCUs are obtained after several years of investment and 
project implementation. The costs of nursery establishment and tending of 
planted seedlings are beyond what UWA and or the local communities can afford.

For example, initial reforestation activities for the Kibale project were funded by 
NORAD (IUCN and Ministry of Environment Protection, 1990) and IUCN (Ministry 
of Environment Protection, 1990) because UWA could not afford it.  By 1993, IUCN 
invited Face to help them with investment into ARR activities and the initial cost 
for the first year alone was €13,138 which  by the year 2010 has turned into a €3 
million investment by Face - understandably unaffordable for both UWA and local 
communities.   
 
b) Institutional barriers 
Despite the environmental needs, there has been no institution with requisite 
capacity to implement a program of forest restoration on the proposed project 
sites. Restoration of these degraded areas could not occur in the absence of 
human resource capacity of UWA to enforce the protection laws on the National 
Park. Infrastructure is another barrier for afforestation project of this magnitude. 
The project activities in Kibale for example has had to build offices and staff 
houses, purchase big items such as project vehicles, motorcycles, water pump,  
electricity generator and road maintenance (>€75,00.00 investment) all of which 
were not in place before the start of  project activities.  Infrastructures such as 
these and roads are not only necessary but critical for a successful remote-based 
project like Kibale.  
 
c) Technological barriers 
Both technical and technological barriers represent a complete array of 
shortcomings in the successful establishment of either small or large scale ARR 
project activities. Interviews with the project team of UWA, District officials and 
local communities indicate that there is usually limited access to required inputs 
and management. Lack of knowledge on the quality seed sources and lack of skills 
for producing high quality seedlings at a large scale are a major setback. For 
successful tree planting as well as for preventing planted trees from being subject 
to fire, severe competition with grasses, etc,  the project team would have to 
overcome a wide array of technical and technological barriers for a successful 
reforestation project.  
 
d) First of a kind project barrier 
Implementing an ARR project at a date earlier than the Kyoto Protocol,  at a large 
scale and in operational partnership with UWA would make it a first of its kind.  
There are no records of such a project in Uganda. And even those that exist, none 
of them have been implemented with the objective of establishing a highly 
degraded natural forest through direct plantation of native species. As a 
consequence, such a project would have to overcome significant barriers in the 
establishment, implementation and monitoring phases as its project staff would 
have no experience and no other existing projects to learn from. 
 
Sub-step 2b: Elimination of land use scenarios that are prevented by the identified 
barriers:  
The fourth land use scenario regarding afforestation of the lands within the 
project area performed without being registered as an ARR VCS project activity is

eliminated from consideration because it is prevented by all the barriers outlined 
in sub-step 2a. On the other hand, continuation of pre-project scenarios 1-3 are not 
prevented by any of the barriers listed above in sub-step 2a.  
 
Sub-step 2c: Determination of baseline scenarios allowed by the barrier analysis:  
As stated in sub-step 2b above, continuation of the pre-project land use scenarios 
1-3 which includes different levels of encroachment and seasonal fires is not 
prevented by any of the barriers listed above in sub-step 2a.  The qualitative 
analysis to assess the removals by sinks for each of these baseline scenarios is 
described as follows:

1. Continued encroachment at a scale and rate of before project activities 
started 1993 resulting in a mix of grassland, shrubland and banana 
plantations This would mean that the carbon stock stays more or less 
constant at 3.6 Mg/ha  as presented in the  baseline determination report 
of Meijer (1999).  
2. Continued but less intense encroachment assuming that UWA would have 
limited success in keeping encroachers at bay. This would mean that fires 
continue to roam the formerly encroached land and the carbon stock 
would be the result of a mix between agricultural activities, fire and 
partial regeneration of pioneer vegetation (grass and shrubs). The carbon 
stock in this case would be for the mix of shrub, forest and banana and 
round 4.4 Mg/ha (Meijer, 1999).    
3. No human encroachment, assuming that the park would have some 
success in protecting the area, but no investment in forest rehabilitation, 
while widespread and frequent perturbation by fire continues.  The 
resulting fire regime would favour elephant grass which would in turn 
suppress natural regeneration of trees. The carbon stock in this scenario 
would be about 1.1 Mg/ha (Meijer, 1999).  
 
Land use scenario 2 is considered to be most likely conservative baseline scenario, 
i.e. giving the smallest difference with the project scenario 4.4 Mg/ha (Table 2.5.1). 
However, the more conservative figure of 5.2 Mg/ha, belonging to the stratum 
‘banana plantation’, is adopted as the baseline carbon stock to be more 
conservative.

STEP 4. Common practice analysis 
There are a couple of projects being implemented in other regions of Uganda. The 
first is a small scale reforestation project in Rwoho Central Forest Reserve of the 
Nile Basin. The Rwoho project was the first ever Ugandan project to be registered 
under CDM. It is part of a project cluster of 5 similar projects aiming to provide a 
new financing mechanism to overcome the current barriers to establish timber 
plantations in Uganda and to allow communities to benefit from the CDM. In total 
the project activities cover an area of 347.1 ha within Rwoho Central Forest 
Reserve (NFA planting area: 324.9 ha (94 %), community planting area: 22.2 ha (6 
%). The Reserve covers in total an area of 9,100 ha. Based on conservative 
estimates, with a 22 years rotation cycle for all tree species, the project will 
produce 24,421 tCO2-e by 2012. The project allows the involvement of private and 
community-based tree planting initiatives with different investor shares. Due 
diligence, monitoring, validation and verification costs will be shared among the 
project cluster. Based on a successful implementation of the first pilot cluster it is 
planned to extend the portfolio across the country clustered in a number of 
deforested public forest reserves and target regions. Hence, a project design that 
can be easily replicated was developed and the concept will consider options for a 
programmatic approach.

1 Description of Project:  
 
1.1 Project title  
 
Natural High Forest Rehabilitation Project on degraded land of Kibale National 
Park. 
 
1.2 Type/Category of the project  
 
The Natural High Forest Rehabilitation Project on degraded land of Kibale National 
Park falls under the scope of Agriculture Forestry and Other Land Use category 
(AFOLU) and is specifically a Reforestation (R) project type of the ARR category. 
 
This is not a grouped project.  
 
1.3 Estimated amount of emission reductions over the crediting period 
including project size: 
 
The project is expected to sequester 4,450,862 of tCO2-e during its 60 year 
crediting period. 
 
1.4 A brief description of the project: 
 
The Project activity in Kibale National Park (KNP) is located in western part of 
Uganda and is implemented by Uganda Wildlife Authority (UWA) in cooperation 
with Face the Future (FtF). Due to the high precipitation, complex landform and 
undulating valleys, as well as continual human disturbance (fire, grazing, charcoal 
production and cultivation) and poor land management, the area has been 
subjected to severe degradation of the surrounding vegetation as well as soil 
erosion. The project contributes to climate change mitigation by sequestering 
GHGs in sinks through tree planting and assisted natural regeneration activities. 
 
The Kibale National Park is considered to contain some of the highest biological 
diversity in Uganda. There are at least 372 bird species, 4 species of wild cats and 
contains at least 351 tree species (Howard, 1996). This National Park also supports 
an exceptionally diverse and abundant primate fauna: 13 species of primates are 
found within the park, which is 67 % of the country’s total species (IUCN, 1988). 
Kibale may contain the only viable population of red colobus monkey in Uganda. 
Furthermore, Kibale National Park is home to one of the largest chimpanzee 
populations in the world. The park is also home to a high number of butterfly and 
night moth species. Other prominent animal species are bushbucks and African 
elephants, as well as many reptile species such as the African rock python.  
 
The purpose of the proposed ARR VCS project activity is to realize multiple socio-
economic and environmental benefits (local community development, climate

change mitigation, biodiversity conservation and soil erosion control) through 
restoring forest vegetation on degraded lands.  
 
Specific project objectives are to:

• Restore the integrity of the degraded forest ecosystems in the National 
Park and thereby enhance biodiversity conservation and control of soil 
erosion. This is achieved by replanting the degraded areas with locally 
occurring indigenous trees species. 
• Transfer forestry knowledge and skills to the local communities with an 
aim to make them environmental ambassadors of the project. 
• Provide employment opportunities to the communities adjacent to the 
park.  
• Provide income generating opportunities by encouraging the 
establishment of locally owned and operated nurseries where seedlings 
are raised and later sold to the ARR VCS project. 
• Promote regeneration of natural vegetation in the forest interior areas by 
creating a forested zone around the edge of the park which will act as a 
buffer to relieve the interior areas of pressure from agents of 
deforestation and degradation (i.e. anthropogenically caused fires).  
 
To achieve these objectives, the following VCS ARR project activity is proposed: 
 
Rehabilitation of 6,213 ha of degraded forest inside Kibale National Park through 
reforestation using model indigenous species such as Albizzia qummifera, Bridelia 
micrantha, Cordia africana, Cordia millenii, Croton macrostachyus, Croton 
megalocarpus, Erythrina abyssinica, Ficus natalensis, Mimusopsis bagshawei, Prunus 
africana, Spathodea campanulata,  Sapium ellipticum, and Warburgia ugandensis. 
These are fast growing species and have been proven to outgrow the grasses to 
avoid being suffocated and are resistant to grass root competition.  
 
 
1.5 Project location including geographic and physical information 
allowing the unique identification and delineation of the specific 
extent of the project: 
 
Location of the proposed ARR VCS project activity: 
The project activity is located in western Uganda, near the base of the Rwenzori 
Mountains and about 200 km north of the equator (Figure 1.5.1). It falls into 
Kabarole district and is within half an hour’s drive from Fort Portal town.

1.7 Conditions prior to project initiation: 
 
Due to the high precipitation, complex landform and undulating valleys, as well as 
continual human disturbance (fire, grazing, charcoal production and cultivation) 
and poor land management, the area has been subjected to severe degradation 
of the surrounding vegetation as well as soil erosion. 
 
Up until the 1960s, the project area was characterised by an intact natural high 
forest. However, due to changes in government (1970-1980s) and the 
consequential lack of implementation of policies, this forest was gradually 
deforested. The reserve has been subjected to continued degradation, especially 
over the last few decades where a significant increase in subsistence activities, 
such as cultivation and grazing activities, fuel-wood collection, and charcoal 
production have been witnessed, reducing a denser rainforest to a landscape with 
scarce pockets of trees. By 1980s, the proposed ARR VCS project area had 
become non-forest land. Furthermore, continued human activities such as 
frequent burning, grazing, shifting cultivation, fuel wood collection resulted in 
severe forest and soil degradation. This rendered the areas useless and were 
consequently abandoned.  
 
To demonstrate that the land within the project boundary is eligible for an ARR 
VCS project activity, steps outlined in the ‘Procedures to define the eligibility of 
lands for forestation and reforestation CDM project activities, version 1’ were 
followed. The applicable step for the Kibale project was (a) (i) as follows:

forest:

Vegetation on the land is below the forest national thresholds (crown 
cover, tree height and minimum land area) for the forest definition 
under decisions 11/CP.7 and 19/CP.9 as communicated by the 
respective DNA.

1.8 A description of how the project will achieve GHG emission reductions 
and/or removal enhancements: 
 
The project contributes to climate change mitigation by sequestering GHGs in 
sinks through assisted natural regeneration activities that aim to promote 
regeneration of natural vegetation in the forest interior areas by creating a 
forested zone around the edge of the park which will act as a buffer to relieve the 
interior areas of pressure from agents of deforestation and degradation (i.e. 
anthropogenically caused fires).

To achieve these objectives, the following VCS ARR project activity is proposed: 
 
Rehabilitation of 6,212 ha of degraded forest inside Kibale National Park through 
reforestation using model indigenous species. 
 
1.9 Project technologies, products, services and the expected level of 
activity:  
 
1.9.1 Technology to be employed by the proposed ARR VCS project activity: 
The technological practices currently implemented and to be implemented in the 
near future in the VCS ARR project are outlined below.

1. Identification of lands suitable for project 
The project utilized remote sensing maps generated from 1989, 2003 and 2004 
satellite images. In addition to this, a land evaluation for natural regeneration map 
1996 by Jungerius, and a lands cover stratification map Sheet/2 1996 from the 
Uganda Department of Lands and Surveys were utilized to identify lands suitable 
for the project activity. The data was organized using a geographic information 
system database. Just before planting, an advanced survey through physical 
observation was carried out by UWA staff.

2. Nursery 
The planting stock is derived from tree seedlings collected in the wild and nursery 
stock grown from seed. The wildlings are collected from within the park, potted 
out, and grown on in the project’s nursery before being planted out. Wildlings 
collection is considered unlikely to have a serious long-term impact on the ecology 
and vegetation dynamics of the collection area. Mature forest trees vary in the 
amount and frequency of seed produced, but most will produce many hundreds 
of thousands of propagules spread over a period of several decades. See Section 
1.9.2  for tree species. Activities required for proper growth of seedlings are 
shown in Table 1.9.1.1 Also seedlings raised in communities are purchased, as a 
way of promoting further income generation activities within the local 
communities.

Spot slashing: In the second year after planting, spot slashing was carried out at 
intervals of three months in the second and third year. In the fourth and fifth year, 
spot slashing was carried   at four month intervals to harden off planted crop and 
reduce maintenance costs.  
 
Spot hoeing: this was only carried out in the new crop during the second rains 
after planting. This was done in order to allow easy penetration of water and 
reduce weed competition. 
 
Fire Protection:  Fires are a major factor preventing forest regeneration. Elephant 
grass and spear grass provide excellent combustible material especially during the 
dry seasons. Planted areas are completely surrounded by a 15 m external fire line 
or by non-combustible riverine vegetation. In the centre of each 15 m firebreak 4 
m are scrapped clean of all vegetation. Furthermore, each compartment is divided 
into manageable blocks, which are separated by 10 m wide internal fire lines. 
Three meters of all internal fire lines is also scrapped clean. All fire lines are 
accessible by cars during the dry season. Training and retraining workers in fire 
fighting techniques is done. Another vital component of fire protection is fire 
awareness campaigns among the local populations neighbouring the park, 
including schools.   
 
GIS technology:

Global Positioning System (GPS) has been extensively employed in the ARR VCS 
project’s activities. Examples of GPS technology usage include, but are not limited 
to, the establishment of planted compartments, permanent sample plots, 
navigation to permanent plots and demarcation of park boundary. GIS has been 
used in the planning, carbon monitoring and verification of the project’s activities.  
 
 
1.9.2  Transfer of technology/know-how: 
The Batoro and Bakiga communities are traditionally subsistence farmers who 
grow crops such as bananas, groundnuts, sweet potatoes and sugar cane. They 
did not have knowledge of reforestation and there was therefore a need to train 
them in forestry techniques; including seed collection, nursery management, 
planting, maintenance and protection.  The knowledge that the local communities 
acquired helped them to raise tree seedlings which they plant in their own 
farmlands and sold to the project in order to improve their income levels. Since 
the beginning of the project, UWA has carried out on-the-job training for over 300 
local community members who are employed on a perennial basis by the project 
to carry out rehabilitation programs. 
 
Furthermore, UWA members of staff implementing the project activities are also 
trained to gain professional skills in different fields such as environmental 
management, finance and accounting and human resource management.

Chrysophyllum albidum (Sapotaceae family):  A tall and straight evergreen tree 
averaging 50 m in height with a dominant canopy; present in mixed parts of Kibale 
forest.  The leaves are compound (oval-oblong shape) with an albidum (white or 
silvery - gray) under surface on mature leaves; the species is an intermediate 
requiring spacious shade when young. 
Propagation: It is propagated from wildings and seeds.   
Uses: fuel wood, timber and food. 
 
Cordia africana/abyssinica (Boraginaceae family): A deciduous tree averaging 15-25 
m in height, often with a crooked trunk. It tolerates a variety of soil types and is 
common in moist forests, riverine galleries and wooded grasslands. Leaves are 
large (16 cm) and oval in shape, with a rounded base.    
Propagation: It is propagated from wildlings and seeds.  
Uses: fuel wood, timber, medicine, fodder, bee forage and soil mulch. 
 
Cordia mellenii/ugandensis (Boraginaceae family): A large tree measuring 30-45 m 
in height, with a wavy trunk rarely straight and a spreading crown. The leaves are 
large (16 x 13 cm) round, alternate with rounded tips and a heart shaped base. 
Propagation: It is propagated from wildings and seeds.  
Uses: timber, carving, fodder, bee forage and soil mulch. 
 
Croton macrostachys (Euphorbiaceae family): A deciduous tree with a rounded 
open crown formed by large spreading branches.  The leaves are large, soft and 
heart-shaped.  It is a fast growing species in areas with deep soils and high rainfall 
(1,100–2,500 masl). 
Propagation:  It is propagated from primarily seeds, and occasionally from 
wildlings.   
Uses: timber, poles, medicine, folder, soil conservation.  Use as a fuelwood is 
limited because of the unpleasant spicy odour released from the poisonous sap. 
 
Croton megalocarpus  (Euphorbiaceae family): A semi - deciduous forest tree with 
an average height of 30 m and a light shade crown.  It is widespread in Kibale 
forest mostly in semi - humid habitats of 100–2,500 masl.  It is fast growing in 
areas with deep soils.  Its leaves are of variable sizes, with a dull green upper 
surface and pole silvery underside. 
Propagation:  It is propagated through direct sowing of seeds in pots.   
Uses: timber, medicine and fuel wood. 
 
Diospyros mespiliformis: A medium to large tree up to 25 m in height with a grey 
bark, which is rough and squared. Its leaves are a shiny dark green and alternate. 
Its flowers are fragrant: male flowers are clustered while female flowers are 
solitary. The resulting fruit is rounded in shape to 2-5 cm in a calyx cup, yellow and 
later purple.  The pulp is soft and sweet with brown, hairy seeds. The wood is 
black and pale after felling. 
Propagation: It is propagated from seedlings and wildlings. 
Uses: Firewood, charcoal, timber, food (fruit; dry, fresh, fermented drink), 
medicine (bark, roots, fruits) bee forage shade and ornamental.

Erythrina abyssinica (Papilionaceae family): A deciduous savannah woodland and 
grassland tree with a short trunk and thick spreading branches forming a rounded 
canopy at an average of 10m in height.  Its round leaves are compound, with three 
leaflets, the largest being 15 cm in diameter,  
Propagation: Propagation is from seeds, wildlings and cuttings taken during the 
rainy season. The tree is resistant to fire and termites.   
Uses: carving, medicine, soil conservation, floats for fish nets, corks.

Ficus natalensis (Moraceae family): An evergreen tree/shrub of up to 30 m in 
height with upright branches and a dense dropping crown.  It grows in a wide 
range of climates, and in both wet and dry areas of 10-2,200 masl. 
Propagation: Propagation is from cuttings which sprout/coppice vigorously.  
Uses: medicine, fuel wood and bark cloth.

Funtumia elastic: A forest tree which grows up to 40 cm in height with a straight 
cylindrical bole and no buttress. The bark is smooth and thin. It exudes abundant 
cream coloured latex which dries to a small ball if rubbed between the fingers. 
The leaves are broadly oval, opposite, dark green and leathery. Flowers are 
yellow-white, fragrant, and in dense shoot groups. Fruits develop as a pair of 
woody, flat follicles of 30cm. Seeds have long white hairs at one end. 
Propagation:  It is propagated from seeds and wildlings. 
Uses: Unknown.

Lovoa trichiliodes/L. brownii : Lovoa trichiliodes/L. brownii : An evergreen tree of 
40m in height. The trunk is straight or wavy with a small or spreading dark crown. 
Buttresses usually absent, but the trunk may spread out at the base.  The bark is 
thin and smooth, brown, and sometimes dark and fissured in older trees, strongly 
scented if cut. Leaves; even pinnate on stalks to 24cm, stalk flat or winged 
between leaflet pairs, 6-12 leaflets, the same size at the base, about 10cm long 
with about 20 closely spaced side veins each side.  Small white flowers are 
abundant in large heads of 30cm. The fruit is present as a brown hanging capsule.  
Propagation: It is propagated from seeds and wildings. 
Uses: Firewood, timber (furniture, doors, windows), charcoal and ornamental.  
 
Markhamia platycalyx (Bignomaceae family): Slender boled tree of 24m in height. 
Its stem is fluted towards the base; the crown is irregular, and the bark is 
grey/brown and flaking in irregular strips and patches. Leaves; compound pinnate 
with 7-11 leaflets, often in bunches, thin and wavy, each leaflets to 10 cm, wider at 
the tip. . Flowers; Bright yellow clusters, each trumpet shaped with orange red 
strips in the throat, buds furry, splitting in one side.. The fruit capsule grows up to 
1.2 m long and 1.9 cm broad, with oblong seeds about 2.5 cm long including the 
yellow to white wood wings. 
Propagation: It is propagated from seeds and wildlings. 
Uses:  Firewood, timber, poles, posts, tool handles, medicine (leaves), bee forage, 
shade, and soil conservation ornamental.

Mimusops bagshawei (Sapotaceae family): A tall straight tree reaching 50m in 
height with a large spreading crown often fluted at the base. It is common in low 
and upland rain forests. The leaves are oval and often wide at the tip, and shiny 
dark green on the superior side, pale dull underneath. 
Propagation: It is propagated from seeds and wildlings. 
Uses: fuel wood, timber, medicine, fodder, bee forage. 
 
Prunus african/Pygeum africana (Rosaceae family): An evergreen tree of up to 40m 
in height occurring in moist mixed tropical rain forests, forest edges and 
gallery/valley forests of 1,100–2,000 masl. Its leaves are a leathery glossy dark 
green on branches dotted with breathing pores. 
Propagation: It is propagated from seeds and wildlings. It is a very fast growing, 
pioneering species often present in secondary succession vegetation.  It requires 
light and is often browsed by game.  
Uses: fuel wood, timber and medicine. 
 
Sapium ellipticum: A small to medium sized deciduous tree occasionally reaching 
20m in height. The bark is light brown/black and rough; often with drooping 
branches. Its leaves are long and oval in shape; dark green on the upper side, pale 
on the underside, turning dark red before falling. Flowers have no petals or sepals 
and are catkin-like with long spikes (5-10 cm) long, the upper part with tiny male 
flowers each with yellow stamens. Its fruit has a two-part red capsule about 1cm 
across, which opens up to set free seeds. The seeds are often eaten by insect 
larvae. 
Propagation: It is propagated from seeds and wildlings 
Uses: Firewood, farm tool handles, medicine (leaves & roots) and ornamental.

1.11 Identification of risks that may substantially affect the project’s GHG 
emission reductions or removal enhancements: 
 
Non-permanence risk assessment was carried out using the VCS’  “AFOLU Non-
Permanence Risk Tool” version 3 of 8 March 2011.  According to this tool, the 
project activity was rated at a low risk after yielding a 8.5% of buffer requirement. 
The project has a system in place to identify risks and established targets to 
reduce any non-permanent risks. Procedures have been developed and 
responsibilities are well assigned with internal auditing, reviews and training in 
place.  The project also has a well qualified, experienced local management team 
in place to ensure that the project activities are implemented effectively.  The land 
planned for the project activity is wholly contained within a national park.  Based 
on the Sections 3,4 and 5 of the Uganda Wildlife Statute, the national park is fully 
owned by the government of Uganda under the UWA Act and mandated by 
Uganda Wildlife Authority on behalf of Uganda government and all Ugandans. 
Therefore, UWA has full control over the entire project lands. Additionally, the 
project will hold a 10%  VCS buffer in reserve for use in case of any loss of 
permanence.   
 
Reference is hereby made to the detailed VCS report called  “Non-Permanence Risk 
Report: Natural High Forest Rehabilitation Project on degraded land of Kibale 
National Park” for more information.   
 
 
1.12 Demonstration to confirm that the project was not implemented to 
create GHG emissions primarily for the purpose of its subsequent 
removal or destruction.  
 
 At the time the project started, in 1995, carbon credits were not a commodity and 
the concept was unheard of. Face became involved in 1994 and did not invest in 
forest destruction but in forest restoration. Instead, deforestation that took place 
in the UWA-Face project area was as a result of  encroachment by local  
communities in the period between 1970 and 1985 (Okonya, 1993). For almost  30 
years local communities were farming within the Forest Reserve, grazing cattle, 
growing maize and bananas. There was no productively managed forest in the 
area. In 1993 all inhabitants and encroachers within the boundaries of the National 
Park were were re-settled  in Kibaale District,  approximately 100 km from Kibale 
National Park (FSC, 2010; General Management Plan of Kibale National Park, 2003-
2013).  These statements are further substantiated by the Figures 1.7.1 and 1.7.2 
presented earlier in the PD. 
 
The purpose of the project is to reforest degraded lands and to promote natural 
regeneration. The project was not implemented to create GHG emissions hence 
no clearing of forest for creation of VCU’s took place.

2.4 Description of how the baseline scenario is identified and description 
of the identified baseline scenario:

The “Combined tool to identify the baseline scenario and demonstrate 
additionality in ARR CDM project activities” is used to both identify  the baseline 
scenario. As will be demonstrated in Section 2.5, the most likely baseline scenario 
in the project area is scenario 2: less encroachment. This scenario assumes that 
UWA would have limited success in keeping encroachers at bay. This would mean that 
fires continue to roam the formerly encroached land and the carbon stock would be the 
result of a mix between agricultural activities, fire and partial regeneration of pioneer 
vegetation (grass and shrubs). The carbon stock in this case would be for the mix of 
shrub, forest and banana plantations. 
 
2.5 Description of how the emissions of GHG by source in baseline 
scenario are reduced below those that would have occurred in the

absence of the project activity (assessment and demonstration of 
additionality): 
 
The “Combined tool to identify the baseline scenario and demonstrate 
additionality in ARR CDM project activities” is used to both identify  the baseline 
scenario and to demonstrate additionally: 
 
STEP 0: Preliminary screening based on the starting date of the ARR project 
activity 
 
The proposed ARR VCS project was started in 1995 and since then, it has applied 
an externally reviewed methodology and engaged independent carbon 
monitoring experts to assess and quantify the project’s baseline scenario and net 
emissions reductions or removals resulting in carbon crediting under the SGS 
standard. In 2003 Face contracted the certification Société Générale de 
Surveillance (SGS) to validate and verify Kibale, based on SGS’ GHG Validation and 
Verification program. In the absence of an international standard defined or 
accepted by the UNFCCC Secretariat, SGS had prepared a set of criteria based on 
Decision 17/C.P7 of the Marrakech accords. These criteria act as a standard and the 
Kibale project was validated against it twice: in 2003 and 2008 respectively. 
Reports of these assessments were published in 2004 and 2009. Since then, 
project activity has been geared towards future crediting under VCS.  The 
incentive of planned sale of GHG emission allowances is evidenced in the steps 
further below of the additionality test. Without the GHG allowance sales, the 
project would not be economically attractive, and would face significant barriers.  
 
STEP 1: Identification of alternative land use scenarios to the proposed ARR VCS 
project activity 
 
Sub-step 1a: Identification of credible alternative land use scenarios to the project 
activity 
Since the lands to be planted are restricted to forestry purposes by government, 
other land uses are practically impossible, therefore the identified alternative land 
uses include three that were historically possible and one that relates to 
afforestation as recommended by the tool.

1. Continued encroachment at a scale and rate  of before project activities 
started 1993 This alternative comprises of a mix of grassland, shrub land 
and banana plantations.  
2. Continued but less intensive encroachment, assuming that UWA would 
have limited success in keeping encroachers at bay. This would mean that 
fires continue to roam the formerly encroached land and the carbon stock 
would be the result of a mix between agricultural activities, fire and partial 
regeneration of pioneer vegetation (grass, shrubs and bananas).

There are a couple of projects being implemented in other regions of Uganda. The 
first is a small scale reforestation project in Rwoho Central Forest Reserve of the 
Nile Basin. The Rwoho project was the first ever Ugandan project to be registered 
under CDM. It is part of a project cluster of 5 similar projects aiming to provide a 
new financing mechanism to overcome the current barriers to establish timber 
plantations in Uganda and to allow communities to benefit from the CDM. In total 
the project activities cover an area of 347.1 ha within Rwoho Central Forest 
Reserve (NFA planting area: 324.9 ha (94 %), community planting area: 22.2 ha (6 
%). The Reserve covers in total an area of 9,100 ha. Based on conservative 
estimates, with a 22 years rotation cycle for all tree species, the project will 
produce 24,421 tCO2-e by 2012. The project allows the involvement of private and 
community-based tree planting initiatives with different investor shares. Due 
diligence, monitoring, validation and verification costs will be shared among the 
project cluster. Based on a successful implementation of the first pilot cluster it is 
planned to extend the portfolio across the country clustered in a number of 
deforested public forest reserves and target regions. Hence, a project design that 
can be easily replicated was developed and the concept will consider options for a 
programmatic approach. 
 
The other reforestation activity is the Community Reforestation Project in the 
Albertine Rift valley region which is currently working with established groups of 
farmers in the Albertine Rift region of Uganda to plant agroforestry and small

scale plantations. Additional activities include the planting of mixed native 
woodlot for timber - including mahogany, cedar, African cherry, laurel, and silk 
trees - along with boundary planting for fuel wood and fruit. This region has been 
classified as a biological hotspot according to Conservation International and is 
also the home to the Rwenzori Mountains which are a UNESCO World Heritage 
site. Furthermore, approximately 50,000 metric tons of CO2 are reduced each 
year, and the Project has been registered with the voluntary carbon standard 
called Plan Vivo. The project, which was established in 2003, is now looking to 
expand into new communities and local field officers are currently setting up 
training for newly recruited farmers in these new regions. With this in mind, all the 
community forestry management groups "have signed agreements with the 
National Forest Authority to participate in the management of Forest Reserves 
(Budongo and Bugoma). In addition, two groups in Masindi are in the final stages 
of acquiring titles of Communal Ownership for Ongo and Alimugonza communal 
forests. The communities need availability of a long term source of income to 
facilitate the forest management activities. It is envisaged that carbon finance will 
provide that source of income." 
 
Project activities similar to Kibale’s magnitude and approach not been 
implemented in the region. The project objective is to establish degraded area of 
natural high forest inside the Kibale National Park. Natural forest rehabilitation is 
not common in Uganda as many plantations are of exotic species. Therefore, no 
projects of this type have been reported, and therefore this can be recognized as 
a first of its kind project.

3.4 Description of the monitoring plan

3.4.1  Information on how geographic coordinates of the project boundary are 
established, recorded and archived:  
 
The project boundary is used to delineate the project area. The location of each 
node of the project boundary will be measured during fieldwork and archived in 
the database. The project boundary is monitored at during events such as site 
preparation, planting, permanent sampling operations, fire monitoring events, 
carbon monitoring campaign, etc., during which compartment IDs and 
compartment areas are required to be entered. 
 
Two major activities are implemented with regards to the monitoring of the 
project boundary.  
 
One of the major activities for monitoring utilizes a computer program called 
MONIS (Monitoring and Information System) which was developed with the 
specific aim to monitor the progress of the project over the lifetime of the 
contract. The program makes use of satellite images, ground photographs and 
topographic maps of the region. In addition to this program, Geographic 
Positioning System (GPS) is utilized in order to locate the specific boundaries of 
the project area and the National Park at large.  An in-house training program was 
developed and implemented for relevant staff members and they were trained on 
the use of GPS technology. In order to store basic data in a logical order, data 
entry into MONIS is carried out on a monthly basis after the monthly reports have 
been submitted from the field.  
 
The second major activity that is carried out is mapping of project and planted 
compartment boundaries using a hand-held GPS. Coordinates at each turning 
point on the compartment boundary are recorded in order to show proper 
boundaries of planted areas and to determine the actual planted areas. Mapping 
is carried out every year after planting targets have been achieved. The end 
product of the mapping exercises are maps of the rehabilitated areas.  
 
All spatial data are archived at the UWA-Face office in Kibale and at the Face the 
Future office in the Netherlands.

3.4.2.5 Plot design 
 
Each inventory plot (Figure 3.4.2.5) was composed of four circles with an area of 
500 m2 each (i.e. 2 000 m2 altogether). Amongst these circles, one circle acts as a 
key circle which contains an additional concentric subplot to measure smaller 
trees and another small circle to assess the amount of tree regeneration. The 
applied limits for sub-circles and tree size specified for the carbon monitoring 
project in Uganda are shown in Table 3.4.2.5.

entire plot. Trees equal or greater than 15 cm of DBH are measured in the light 
gray circle. Trees equal or greater than 5 cm of DBH are measured in the inner 
dark gray circle. 
 
Natural regeneration within the plots was surveyed only in the regeneration circle 
(2 m radius), located 8 m to the North from plot centre. If regeneration is present, 
height and species were described.  A tree is classified as regeneration only if its 
DBH is less than 50 mm and has a height greater than 10 cm.

3.4.2.6 Plot Monumentation  
 
In order to comply with the requirement of the methodology (AR-ACM0001-
Version 05.0.0) for permanent sampling plots, all inventory plots are measured in 
a local Cartesian co-ordinate system with the center in the middle of inventory 
plot. The project utilizes both the Laser and GPS technologies to locate plot 
centers. The GPS is used in Global Coordinate System (i.e. on the navigation plot) 
where as the Laser is utilized on both the local and global coordinate systems. The 
Laser is reliable for navigation under canopy, provides a precise navigation to the 
plot center and is utilized for all measurements carried out within the inventory 
plot.  
 
From the  center of an inventory plot, a position of marked tree is measured. This 
marked tree is then painted and if necessary some more descriptive comments 
are entered into the database. Selection of the tree to be painted is based on the 
size and type of the tree. For example , a tree of 20cm DBH,  belonging to the 
climax species group and not edible to wildlife, is preferably selected because it is 
more likely to still be alive during the next carbon monitoring campaign, 5 years 
later.  Therefore, during the repeated measurements the geo-reference is taken 
from the painted tree. This means that upon reaching the inventory plot, the Field 
Team immediately searches around for painted tree and uses the positioning 
routine to get a reference from it.  
 
In order to improve the permanent visibility of the plots and especially the plot 
centres, concrete markers will be placed in the plot centres by the end of 2011.   
 
3.4.2.7 Precision requirements 
 
The number of permanent sampling plots and the targeted precision level for the 
biomass estimation is ± 10% of the mean at a 90% confidence level and was 
determined using the approved CDM  tool for “Calculation of the number of 
sample plots for measurements within A/R CDM project activities”  version 02.1.0 as 
required by the CDM methodology AR-ACM0001, version 05.0.0.

The carbon pools in the baseline scenario are in a steady state. Therefore no 
monitoring of baseline net GHG removals is carried out.  
 
3.4.2.9 Monitoring of the actual net GHG removals by sinks 
 
Monitoring of the actual net GHG removals by sinks in the planted compartments 
takes place every five years.  In Kibale, these were carried out in 2003 and 2008, 
with an exception of  2011 which took only  3 years between 2008 and 2011. This 
exception to the 5-year interval is as a result of the transition from SGS

certification to VCS whereby VCS requires all old projects to be verified before 
September 8, 2011.  After 2011, all future carbon monitoring campaigns will be 
based on the 5-year interval again. Carbon monitoring campaigns are carried out 
following monitoring steps in the Standard Operating Procedures (SOP)  and 
Standard of Quality Control and Quality Assurance developed specifically for 
Kibale (Annex I and II) by  the Czech Republic based Institute of Forest Ecosystem 
Research (IFER).  The SOP contains rules for how DBH measurements and heights 
are carried out in normal terrain as well as under special circumstances such as on 
steep slopes, for slanted trees, etc. The procedures are described using a step-
wise approach, where steps are accompanied with specific pictures and 
screenshots. The content of the SOP is complementary with the content of the 
monitoring training sessions given to inventory teams.

The project activity in Kibale National Park (KNP) is located in the western part of Uganda and is 
implemented by Uganda Wildlife Authority in cooperation with Face the Future. Due to the high precipitation, 
complex landform and undulating valleys, as well as continual human disturbance (fire, grazing, charcoal 
production and cultivation) and poor land management, the area has been subjected to severe degradation 
of the vegetation and soil erosion. The project contributes to climate change mitigation by sequestering 
GHGs in sinks through planting of indigenous tree species and assisted natural regeneration activities. The 
purpose of the project activity is to realize multiple socio-economic and environmental benefits (climate 
change mitigation, biodiversity conservation, local community development and soil erosion control) 
through restoring forest vegetation on degraded lands.

this carbon monitoring campaign since the reforestation activities in these areas were done through 3rd 
party investments. Therefore this monitoring campaign includes 2,755 ha of replanted area and 2,593 ha 
of regeneration area.

the 28th of February 2017, resulted in a net emission removal of 240,850 t CO2-e.

Since the lands to be planted are restricted to forestry purposes by government,

and banana plantations.

have limited success in keeping encroachers at bay. This would mean that 
fires continue to roam the formerly encroached land and the carbon stock 
would be the result of a mix between agricultural activities, fire and partial 
regeneration of pioneer vegetation (grass, shrubs and bananas).

STEP 4. Common practice analysis 
There are a couple of projects being implemented in other regions of Uganda. The 
first is a small scale reforestation project in Rwoho Central Forest Reserve of the 
Nile Basin. The Rwoho project was the first ever Ugandan project to be registered 
under CDM. It is part of a project cluster of 5 similar projects aiming to provide a 
new financing mechanism to overcome the current barriers to establish timber 
plantations in Uganda and to allow communities to benefit from the CDM. In total 
the project activities cover an area of 347.1 ha within Rwoho Central Forest 
Reserve (NFA planting area: 324.9 ha (94 %), community planting area: 22.2 ha (6 
%). The Reserve covers in total an area of 9,100 ha. Based on conservative 
estimates, with a 22 years rotation cycle for all tree species, the project will 
produce 24,421 tCO2-e by 2012. The project allows the involvement of private and 
community-based tree planting initiatives with different investor shares. Due 
diligence, monitoring, validation and verification costs will be shared among the 
project cluster. Based on a successful implementation of the first pilot cluster it is 
planned to extend the portfolio across the country clustered in a number of 
deforested public forest reserves and target regions. Hence, a project design that 
can be easily replicated was developed and the concept will consider options for a 
programmatic approach. 
 
The other reforestation activity is the Community Reforestation Project in the 
Albertine Rift valley region which is currently working with established groups of 
farmers in the Albertine Rift region of Uganda to plant agroforestry and small

scale plantations. Additional activities include the planting of mixed native 
woodlot for timber - including mahogany, cedar, African cherry, laurel, and silk 
trees - along with boundary planting for fuel wood and fruit. This region has been 
classified as a biological hotspot according to Conservation International and is 
also the home to the Rwenzori Mountains which are a UNESCO World Heritage 
site. Furthermore, approximately 50,000 metric tons of CO2 are reduced each 
year, and the Project has been registered with the voluntary carbon standard 
called Plan Vivo. The project, which was established in 2003, is now looking to 
expand into new communities and local field officers are currently setting up 
training for newly recruited farmers in these new regions. With this in mind, all the 
community forestry management groups "have signed agreements with the 
National Forest Authority to participate in the management of Forest Reserves 
(Budongo and Bugoma). In addition, two groups in Masindi are in the final stages 
of acquiring titles of Communal Ownership for Ongo and Alimugonza communal 
forests. The communities need availability of a long term source of income to 
facilitate the forest management activities. It is envisaged that carbon finance will 
provide that source of income." 
 
Project activities similar to Kibale’s magnitude and approach not been 
implemented in the region. The project objective is to establish degraded area of 
natural high forest inside the Kibale National Park. Natural forest rehabilitation is 
not common in Uganda as many plantations are of exotic species. Therefore, no 
projects of this type have been reported, and therefore this can be recognized as

In order to comply with the requirement of the methodology (AR-ACM0001-
Version 05.0.0) for permanent sampling plots, all inventory plots are measured in 
a local Cartesian co-ordinate system with the center in the middle of inventory 
plot. The project utilizes both the Laser and GPS technologies to locate plot 
centers. The GPS is used in Global Coordinate System (i.e. on the navigation plot) 
where as the Laser is utilized on both the local and global coordinate systems. The 
Laser is reliable for navigation under canopy, provides a precise navigation to the 
plot center and is utilized for all measurements carried out within the inventory 
plot.  
 
From the  center of an inventory plot, a position of marked tree is measured. This 
marked tree is then painted and if necessary some more descriptive comments 
are entered into the database. Selection of the tree to be painted is based on the 
size and type of the tree. For example , a tree of 20cm DBH,  belonging to the 
climax species group and not edible to wildlife, is preferably selected because it is 
more likely to still be alive during the next carbon monitoring campaign, 5 years 
later.  Therefore, during the repeated measurements the geo-reference is taken 
from the painted tree. This means that upon reaching the inventory plot, the Field 
Team immediately searches around for painted tree and uses the positioning 
routine to get a reference from it.  
 
In order to improve the permanent visibility of the plots and especially the plot 
centres, concrete markers will be placed in the plot centres by the end of 2011.

Specific project objectives are to:

• Restore the integrity of the degraded forest ecosystems in the National 
Park and thereby enhance biodiversity conservation and control of soil 
erosion. This is achieved by replanting the degraded areas with locally 
occurring indigenous trees species. 
• Transfer forestry knowledge and skills to the local communities with an 
aim to make them environmental ambassadors of the project. 
• Provide employment opportunities to the communities adjacent to the 
park.  
• Provide income generating opportunities by encouraging the 
establishment of locally owned and operated nurseries where seedlings 
are raised and later sold to the ARR VCS project. 
• Promote regeneration of natural vegetation in the forest interior areas by 
creating a forested zone around the edge of the park which will act as a 
buffer to relieve the interior areas of pressure from agents of 
deforestation and degradation (i.e. anthropogenically caused fires).  
 
To achieve these objectives, the following VCS ARR project activity is proposed: 
 
Rehabilitation of 6,213 ha of degraded forest inside Kibale National Park through 
reforestation using model indigenous species such as Albizzia qummifera, Bridelia 
micrantha, Cordia africana, Cordia millenii, Croton macrostachyus, Croton 
megalocarpus, Erythrina abyssinica, Ficus natalensis, Mimusopsis bagshawei, Prunus 
africana, Spathodea campanulata,  Sapium ellipticum, and Warburgia ugandensis. 
These are fast growing species and have been proven to outgrow the grasses to 
avoid being suffocated and are resistant to grass root competition.

Spot slashing: In the second year after planting, spot slashing was carried out at 
intervals of three months in the second and third year. In the fourth and fifth year, 
spot slashing was carried   at four month intervals to harden off planted crop and 
reduce maintenance costs.  
 
Spot hoeing: this was only carried out in the new crop during the second rains 
after planting. This was done in order to allow easy penetration of water and 
reduce weed competition. 
 
Fire Protection:  Fires are a major factor preventing forest regeneration. Elephant 
grass and spear grass provide excellent combustible material especially during the 
dry seasons. Planted areas are completely surrounded by a 15 m external fire line 
or by non-combustible riverine vegetation. In the centre of each 15 m firebreak 4 
m are scrapped clean of all vegetation. Furthermore, each compartment is divided 
into manageable blocks, which are separated by 10 m wide internal fire lines. 
Three meters of all internal fire lines is also scrapped clean. All fire lines are 
accessible by cars during the dry season. Training and retraining workers in fire 
fighting techniques is done. Another vital component of fire protection is fire 
awareness campaigns among the local populations neighbouring the park, 
including schools.   
 
GIS technology:

Global Positioning System (GPS) has been extensively employed in the ARR VCS 
project’s activities. Examples of GPS technology usage include, but are not limited

• disposal of plastic pots from seedlings 
• collection of wildlings from the forest 
 
However, from 2001 onwards seedlings raised in the communities are purchased,

communities. The nursery farmers raise seedlings adjacent to the project 
nurseries not only for easy supervision by Project staff, but also for proper 
rehabilitation of areas where nursery soil is collected. Plastic pots are generally re-

positive impact, enlarging the habitat for native species, protecting the park’s 
biodiversity and enhancing its tourism value. Native grasslands located in the
